analysis.one_liner: Makes the Bush tax cuts permanent and repeals the estate tax, the minimum tax, and Affordable Care Act taxes.
analysis.headline: A single-sponsor bill to permanently extend the Bush tax cuts, repeal the estate tax and alternative minimum tax, and roll back Affordable Care Act taxes died in committee with no cosponsors and never came to a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make the 2001 and 2003 Bush tax cuts permanent, ending their scheduled 2012 expiration. It would permanently repeal the federal estate tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax, which apply only to large inherited fortunes, and repeal the individual alternative minimum tax. It would also roll back the tobacco tax increase that funds the Children's Health Insurance Program and repeal the tax provisions of the Affordable Care Act, including the individual and employer mandate penalties [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthiest households gain the most: permanent repeal of the estate and gift taxes on large inheritances, permanent lower rates on capital gains and dividends, and permanent elimination of the alternative minimum tax, which falls more on higher earners. Middle- and upper-middle-income families also gain from keeping the Bush-era income tax rates and deductions. Tobacco companies gain from the repeal of the 2009 excise tax increase plus refunds of taxes paid on inventory. Employers with 50 or more workers gain from repeal of the Affordable Care Act penalty for not offering coverage [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy inheritors, investors, and tobacco companies

how_it_helps.text: Permanently extends the individual income tax rates, marriage-penalty relief, child credit, and other provisions of the 2001 and 2003 tax laws that were scheduled to expire at the end of 2012 [S2][S3].
Repeals the estate and generation-skipping transfer taxes for all deaths and transfers after 2010, which benefits heirs of estates large enough to owe these taxes [S2][S3].
Repeals the individual alternative minimum tax, which mainly affects taxpayers with higher incomes or large deductions [S2][S3].

Repeals the 2009 tobacco excise tax increase that funds the Children's Health Insurance Program, and refunds taxes already paid on warehouse inventory, so tobacco products would carry lower federal taxes [S2][S3].
Repeals the Affordable Care Act's revenue provisions and the tax penalties attached to the individual and employer mandates [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury pays for all of it: every provision is a tax cut with no replacement revenue, which would either add to deficits or force later spending cuts or tax increases elsewhere. Repealing the tobacco tax would drain funding for the Children's Health Insurance Program, which covers children in lower-income families. Repealing the Affordable Care Act tax provisions would take away the law's funding and enforcement mechanisms, leaving fewer people with coverage and raising costs for those who stay insured [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and children's health funding

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no offsetting revenue or spending cuts, so it would permanently reduce federal revenue across income tax, estate tax, and health-law taxes at once [S3].
Estate tax repeal applies only to very large estates, so its benefits are concentrated among the wealthiest families, and it would remove a major source of federal revenue [S2][S3].
Repealing the tobacco tax increase would cut the dedicated funding stream for the Children's Health Insurance Program created by that same 2009 law [S2][S3].

Repealing the individual and employer mandate penalties without any replacement would weaken the Affordable Care Act's coverage expansion and its funding, raising the risk of higher premiums for people who remain insured [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Keeping the middle-class portions of the Bush tax cuts has real value for working families, and the bill would spare everyone from the scheduled across-the-board rate increases at the end of 2012. But the bill packages that with permanent estate tax repeal, minimum tax repeal, tobacco tax repeal, and Affordable Care Act tax repeal, none of it paid for, and the largest gains go to the wealthiest households and to tobacco companies. An honest supporter would acknowledge the large, unfinanced cost to the Treasury and the cut to children's health insurance funding.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees in January 2012, one subcommittee took a look in March, and no committee ever approved it or brought it to the floor before Congress ended [S1][S5].

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 23, 2012, by Representative Tim Huelskamp with no cosponsors [S1][S4].
It was referred to the Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, and Energy and Commerce committees [S1][S5].
In March 2012 it was referred to a Ways and Means subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions; no further action was recorded for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or a companion in the Senate, and expired when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the estate and gift taxes on large fortunes remained on the books, and the tobacco tax that funds children's health insurance and the Affordable Care Act's revenue stream were untouched. No constituency gained a new tax break; the main beneficiaries of the outcome are the federal Treasury and the existing funding streams for CHIP and the health law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal treasury and children's health funding

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently extend the Bush tax cuts and repeal the estate tax, alternative minimum tax, tobacco tax increase, and Affordable Care Act taxes [S1][S3].

against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee in March 2012 and never brought it up for a markup or a floor vote; the bill died there [S5].

against.name: House Education and the Workforce and Energy and Commerce Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so no party position was ever tested in a vote [S4][S5].

industries.note: Permanent repeal of the estate and generation-skipping transfer taxes would eliminate federal tax on very large inheritances. The revenue cost falls on all federal taxpayers, while the benefit goes only to heirs of estates large enough to owe the tax [S2][S3].

Repeal of the 2009 excise tax increase would lower federal taxes on tobacco products and refund taxes already paid on warehouse inventory. The tax funds the Children's Health Insurance Program, so the industry gain comes at the cost of that funding stream [S2][S3].

industries.industry: High-income investors and capital gains earners
industries.note: Making the 2003 capital gains and dividend rate cuts permanent locks in lower rates that concentrate their benefit among top earners, with the revenue cost shared by everyone [S2][S3].

Repealing the Affordable Care Act employer mandate penalties would free large employers from the tax for not offering qualifying coverage, shifting more of the coverage burden onto workers and the subsidized market [S2][S3].

Repealing the individual mandate penalties would shrink the pool of newly insured customers created by the health law, reducing insurer revenue, while leaving the rest of the health system's rules in place [S2][S3].
